what_it_does: Modern AI applications often need to find the most similar items in a huge collection of high-dimensional numeric fingerprints called vectors — for example, finding the images most similar to a query photo. Doing this at scale requires reading enormous amounts of data from storage, which is slow and energy-hungry. This paper stores the vectors directly inside stacked NAND flash memory chips (the same type used in SSDs) that have been redesigned to also perform comparisons, so data never needs to travel to a separate processor. The key trick is a two-stage filter: a fast, exact-match stage first cheaply eliminates vectors that clearly do not match, and only the surviving candidates proceed to a slower but more flexible approximate-match stage. This avoids wasting energy comparing a query against irrelevant entries. The system also retrains the vector index to be aware of this filtering step, improving reliability. Details come only from the abstract, so quantitative gains remain to be verified.
